title: The books
hook: the Torah of Musa, the Psalms of Dawud, the Gospel of Isa, the Scrolls of Ibrahim, and the Qur'an

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angels, and your line: made of light. Did you say peace, inside, to a room before you walked into it? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

Here's an unusual article of faith: it asks Muslims to believe in books that may never have sat on their own shelves. The third of the six is the books, kutub in Arabic. Not only the Qur'an at home, perhaps wrapped in cloth on a high shelf. Also a scroll given to Ibrahim. A law given to Musa. Songs given to Dawud. A gospel given to Isa, the name the Qur'an uses for Jesus. Five books, five messengers, one belief that holds them together. Today, the shelf the Qur'an builds.
screen: `BOOKS NEVER ON THE SHELF.` → `FIVE BOOKS, FIVE MESSENGERS.`

segments.voice: First, the names. The Qur'an names the Tawrat, the Torah, given to Musa, Moses. The Zabur, the Psalms, given to Dawud, David; in Pickthall's words, "We imparted unto David the Psalms." The Injil, the Gospel, given to Isa. And at the end of a short surah, a fourth: "Lo! This is in the former scrolls, The Books of Abraham and Moses." With the Qur'an itself, that makes the five. Second, the Qur'an's own description of how they connect. It speaks of itself as confirming what was revealed before it, the Torah and the Gospel among them. In Muslim teaching the message across the books is the same at its heart: worship the One, do good, a day of reckoning is coming. Third, what the belief is and isn't. The belief is in those books as they were revealed to their messengers. The Qur'an is held to be the last book and the measure of the others, and Muslim scholars discuss how the earlier texts reached us. Jews and Christians, of course, read their own scriptures on their own terms. This path just says who holds what. Last, a phrase. In one verse the Arabic reads, word by word, for every term, a book. Pickthall renders it, "For everything there is a time prescribed." Some readers hear in it the same idea as this article of faith: no age was left without a word from its Lord.
screen: `TAWRAT, ZABUR, INJIL, SCROLLS.` · `CONFIRMING WHAT CAME BEFORE.` · `AS THEY WERE REVEALED.` · then, large: `FOR EVERY TERM, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The practice: name the five. Picture a single shelf with five books on it, and set them there one by one. The scrolls of Ibrahim. The Torah of Musa. The Psalms of Dawud. The Gospel of Isa. The Qur'an, brought to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Say each name as you place it. Then look at the whole shelf for a while. If you pray, you can ask to understand what your own book asks of you. If you don't, just rest your eyes on the shelf. The bell holds the time.
Kutub. Books; the plural of kitab. The third article of faith: belief in the books Allah revealed to His messengers. Today's word.

Your line: every age had a book. Today, notice which book sits highest in your own home, and why it ended up there. Tomorrow, the people who carried the books: the messengers. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims affirm belief in the revealed books, naming the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil, the scrolls of Ibrahim and the Qur'an, and a Qur'an at home may be kept on a high shelf, sometimes wrapped in cloth.

fork.setup: how does the Qur'an describe its relation to the earlier books?
options: it confirms what was revealed before it.
it says they were never revealed.
fork.reveal: the Qur'an calls itself confirming what came before, naming the Torah and the Gospel, and Muslims treat it as the last book.

original.note: Arabic: books; the singular is kitab, كتاب.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims have one holy book, the Qur'an.
what it means: the third article of faith is belief in all the books revealed to messengers, with the Qur'an as the last.
what a scholar hears: the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and suhuf of Ibrahim; the Qur'an as confirming and guarding them; and the debate over how the earlier texts reached us.
